body.en: Chapter 5 closed with a real gap: none of Chapters 3–5 handle a forcing term with a jump — a switch flipped at a specific instant, exactly the kind of input real circuits and control systems receive. The Laplace transform closes that gap by trading the differential equation for an algebraic one: differentiation in \( t \) becomes multiplication by \( s \), turning \( ay''+by'+cy=g(t) \) into an equation for \( Y(s) \) that ordinary algebra (plus partial fractions) can solve directly.

For a function \( f(t) \) defined on \( t\ge0 \), the Laplace transform is \[ \mathcal{L}\{f\}(s)=F(s)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-st}f(t)\,dt, \] defined for every \( s \) large enough that the improper integral converges (guaranteed, for instance, whenever \( |f(t)|\le Me^{kt} \) for some constants \( M,k \), by taking \( s>k \)).

label.en: Worked example 6.A — Two transforms from the definition

body.en:
Find \( \mathcal{L}\{1\} \) and \( \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\} \) directly.

\[ \mathcal{L}\{1\}=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dt=\Big[-\frac{e^{-st}}{s}\Big]_0^\infty=0-\Big({-}\frac1s\Big)=\frac1s\quad(s>0). \]

\[ \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}e^{at}\,dt=\int_0^\infty e^{-(s-a)t}\,dt=\frac{1}{s-a}\quad(s>a), \] by the same antiderivative with \( s \) replaced by \( s-a \).

Immediate from linearity of the (improper) integral: \[ \mathcal{L}\{c_1f+c_2g\}=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\big[c_1f(t)+c_2g(t)\big]dt=c_1\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt+c_2\int_0^\infty e^{-st}g(t)\,dt=c_1\mathcal{L}\{f\}+c_2\mathcal{L}\{g\}. \]

Suppose \( f \) is continuous and of exponential order (Definition 6.1's convergence condition) on \( t\ge0 \), with \( \mathcal{L}\{f\}=F(s) \), and \( f' \) is piecewise continuous and also of exponential order — the same regularity Definition 6.1 needs, now required of \( f' \) too, so that \( \mathcal{L}\{f'\} \) itself exists and the integration by parts below is valid. Then \[ \mathcal{L}\{f'\}=sF(s)-f(0). \] Applying this twice (now requiring \( f'' \) piecewise continuous and of exponential order as well), \[ \mathcal{L}\{f''\}=s^2F(s)-sf(0)-f'(0). \]

Integrate by parts with \( u=e^{-st} \), \( dv=f'(t)\,dt \) (so \( du=-se^{-st}dt \), \( v=f(t) \)): \[ \mathcal{L}\{f'\}=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f'(t)\,dt=\Big[e^{-st}f(t)\Big]_0^\infty+s\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt. \] The boundary term at \( \infty \) vanishes (for \( s \) large enough that \( e^{-st}f(t)\to0 \), the same condition Definition 6.1 needs for convergence), and at \( 0 \) it's \( -f(0) \). So \[ \mathcal{L}\{f'\}=-f(0)+sF(s)=sF(s)-f(0). \] For \( f'' \), apply this result to \( f' \) itself (with transform \( \mathcal{L}\{f'\}=sF(s)-f(0) \)): \[ \mathcal{L}\{f''\}=s\mathcal{L}\{f'\}-f'(0)=s\big[sF(s)-f(0)\big]-f'(0)=s^2F(s)-sf(0)-f'(0). \]

label.en: Worked example 6.B — Solving an IVP with the Laplace transform

body.en:
Solve \( y''-3y'+2y=0 \), \( y(0)=1 \), \( y'(0)=0 \) — the same equation type as Chapter 3, now by an entirely different method.

Transform both sides, using Theorem 6.2 and the initial conditions: \[ \big[s^2Y-s(1)-0\big]-3\big[sY-1\big]+2Y=0\;\Longrightarrow\;(s^2-3s+2)Y-s+3=0. \]

Solve for \( Y \): \[ Y(s)=\frac{s-3}{s^2-3s+2}=\frac{s-3}{(s-1)(s-2)}. \] Partial fractions (Linear Algebra Chapter 4's determinant methods aren't needed here — direct substitution suffices): \( \dfrac{s-3}{(s-1)(s-2)}=\dfrac{A}{s-1}+\dfrac{B}{s-2} \). At \( s=1 \): \( A=\dfrac{1-3}{1-2}=2 \). At \( s=2 \): \( B=\dfrac{2-3}{2-1}=-1 \).

So \( Y(s)=\dfrac{2}{s-1}-\dfrac{1}{s-2} \), and reading off Worked example 6.A's transform table in reverse (\( \mathcal{L}\{e^{at}\}=1/(s-a) \)): \[ y(t)=2e^{t}-e^{2t}. \] (Check against Chapter 3's characteristic-equation method: \( r^2-3r+2=(r-1)(r-2)=0 \), \( y=C_1e^t+C_2e^{2t} \); \( y(0)=C_1+C_2=1 \), \( y'(0)=C_1+2C_2=0\Rightarrow C_2=-1,\,C_1=2 \) — the same answer.)

The unit step function \( u(t-a) \) (for \( a\ge0 \)) is \( 0 \) for \( t<a \) and \( 1 \) for \( t\ge a \) — a switch flipped on at time \( a \), exactly the kind of forcing term Chapters 3–5's methods can't handle (it isn't continuous, let alone a polynomial/exponential/trig combination). Its transform: \[ \mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)\}=\int_a^\infty e^{-st}\,dt=\frac{e^{-as}}{s}\quad(s>0), \] and more generally, \( \mathcal{L}\{u(t-a)f(t-a)\}=e^{-as}F(s) \) (the second shifting theorem) — a delayed, shifted copy of \( f \) transforms to \( F(s) \) times a simple exponential factor.

value.en: Transform → solve algebraically for \( Y(s) \) → partial fractions → transform back

body.en:
State (without re-deriving) \( \mathcal{L}\{\cos\omega t\} \) and \( \mathcal{L}\{\sin\omega t\} \).

Solution: Integrating \( e^{-st}\cos\omega t \) and \( e^{-st}\sin\omega t \) by parts twice (the same style of computation as Worked example 6.A) gives the standard pair:

\[ \mathcal{L}\{\cos\omega t\}=\frac{s}{s^2+\omega^2},\qquad\mathcal{L}\{\sin\omega t\}=\frac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}\quad(s>0). \]

Transform both sides of \( y''+4y=\cos2t \), \( y(0)=0,\,y'(0)=0 \), and solve for \( Y(s) \) (don't invert).

Solution: \( \big[s^2Y-0-0\big]+4Y=\dfrac{s}{s^2+4} \Rightarrow (s^2+4)Y=\dfrac{s}{s^2+4} \).

\[ Y(s)=\frac{s}{(s^2+4)^2}. \] (This is the resonance case from Chapter 4 — forcing at the system's own natural frequency \( \omega=2 \) — reappearing here as a repeated factor \( (s^2+4)^2 \) instead of a modified trial function.)

question.en: Practice: Find \( \mathcal{L}\{t\} \) using integration by parts on the definition.

solution.en: \( \mathcal{L}\{t\}=\int_0^\infty te^{-st}\,dt \). By parts, \( u=t,\,dv=e^{-st}dt \Rightarrow du=dt,\,v=-e^{-st}/s \): \( =\big[-te^{-st}/s\big]_0^\infty+\frac1s\int_0^\infty e^{-st}dt=0+\frac1s\cdot\frac1s=\frac{1}{s^2} \) (using Worked example 6.A's \( \mathcal{L}\{1\}=1/s \)).

figure.title: Laplace Kernel Exponential Damping: e^(-st) for s = 1, 2

caption.en: The integral kernel $e^{-st}$ in the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}\,dt$. The decaying exponential suppresses growth, transforming time-domain calculus into algebraic operations in the $s$-domain.

label.en: ⚠️ Common Traps — Derivative Transform Initial Conditions

body.en:
Minus signs in derivative transforms: Recall the derivative formulas: \[ \mathcal{L}\{y'\} = s Y(s) - y(0), \qquad \mathcal{L}\{y''\} = s^2 Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0). \] Both initial condition terms are subtracted. Dropping the initial conditions or using incorrect plus signs corrupts the resulting algebraic equation.

Unit step time shifts: The second shift theorem states \( \mathcal{L}\{g(t)u(t-a)\} = e^{-as}\mathcal{L}\{g(t+a)\} \). Only when the function is already shifted as \( f(t-a)u(t-a) \) does the transform simply equal \( e^{-as}F(s) \).

question.en: Use the Laplace transform to solve the initial value problem \( y' - 2y = 0 \) with \( y(0) = 3 \).

solution.en:
Transforming the ODE: \( sY(s) - y(0) - 2Y(s) = 0 \implies (s - 2)Y(s) = 3 \implies Y(s) = \frac{3}{s - 2} \).

Taking the inverse Laplace transform: \( \mathcal{L}^{-1}\left\{\frac{3}{s - 2}\right\} = 3e^{2t} \). Matching the elementary separable solution \( y(t) = 3e^{2t} \).
